content: A data mart is a specialized subset of a data warehouse, designed to address specific, predefined needs for a particular grouping and configuration of data. Like data warehouses, data marts provide a snapshot of operational data, enabling businesses to analyze past trends and make informed strategic decisions. However, the primary distinction lies in the fact that data marts are tailored to meet specific requirements, making it easier to access relevant information. Within a single organization, there can be multiple data marts, each serving the needs of one or more business units for which it was specifically designed. These data marts may operate independently or be interconnected, depending on whether they share conformed facts and dimensions. If conformed dimensions are used, such as shared definitions for customers or products, the data marts will be related. In some cases, individual departments or business units are considered the sole owners of their respective data marts, including the associated hardware, software, and data. This ownership allows them to manipulate and develop their data independently, without affecting other data marts or the central data warehouse. However, in deployments where shared dimensions are used, this level of autonomy may not apply. When designing a data mart, the star schema or dimensional model is a popular choice. This design allows a relational database to mimic the analytical capabilities of a multidimensional database. Another design option is the snowflake schema. There are several reasons for creating a data mart: It simplifies access to frequently used data. It provides a collective view of data for a specific group of users. It enhances response times for end-users. It is easier to create compared to a full data warehouse. It is less expensive than implementing a full data warehouse. The potential user base is more clearly defined than that of a full data warehouse. A dependent data mart, as defined by the Inmon school of data warehousing, is either a logical subset (view) or a physical subset (extract) of a larger data warehouse. It is isolated for specific purposes, such as: The need for a specialized data model or schema, for example, restructuring data for Online Analytical Processing (OLAP). Performance optimization, such as offloading the data mart to a separate system to improve efficiency or reduce the workload on the central data warehouse. Security, by selectively isolating an authorized subset of data. Expediency, to bypass the governance and authorization processes required to integrate a new application into the enterprise data warehouse. Serving as a proving ground to demonstrate the feasibility and return on investment (ROI) of an application before migrating it to the enterprise data warehouse. Addressing political challenges, such as when a user group has significant influence but limited funding or when the centralized data warehouse team cannot deliver a usable solution. However, the Inmon school also highlights trade-offs associated with data marts. These include limited scalability, duplication of data, potential inconsistencies with other information silos, and the inability to fully leverage enterprise-wide data sources.
